scope: Design-study research, Chicago October 8–10, 1871. Historical geography only. English. Podcast integration deferred.

events.label: Before the alarm
events.title: A city on the edge
events.text: The previous night’s large fire had already strained the firefighters. Strong southwest winds would drive the next fire toward the city centre.

events.label: The first flames
events.title: Fire near DeKoven Street
events.text: The fire begins in or near the O’Leary barn. Its cause remains unknown. Published accounts disagree about the starting time.

events.label: Embers travel
events.title: A second fire takes hold
events.text: Windborne embers start separate fires ahead of the main front. The Tribune describes flames leaping over engines and forcing crews to retreat; Conzen places a second ignition at Bateham’s Mills around 10 p.m.
events.certainty: Scholarly reconstruction; mill location not plotted

events.label: Across the South Branch
events.title: The river cannot contain it
events.text: Separate fires develop in the South Division. The Tribune describes burning fragments landing ahead of the main flames, including around the Armory.

events.label: The Court House
events.title: The alarm tower is reached
events.text: Fire reaches the Court House tower. Prisoners are released before the bell falls through the collapsing building.

events.label: Across the Main Branch
events.title: Fire reaches the North Division
events.text: Conzen’s reconstruction places a new fire north of the river by 2:30 a.m. Several fronts are now spreading through the city.

events.label: The waterworks
events.title: The pumping works fail
events.text: Fire disables the pumping works. Cregier’s 1872 report places the wrecking around 3 a.m.; the museum dates the roof collapse by 3:30.
events.certainty: Time range; descriptions refer to different stages of damage

events.label: Northward
events.title: Beyond the central city
events.text: The museum’s account places the fire at North Avenue by noon, continuing toward Fullerton. These northern areas lie beyond this preview’s map crop.

events.label: After the fire
events.title: Rain over the ruins
events.text: Rain accompanies the fire’s final decline. This endpoint shows documented outcomes, rather than an exact time when every building stopped burning.
events.certainty: Approximate end of the major conflagration

landmarks.name: Court House & City Hall
landmarks.text: City and county government shared this building, with a jail below and a fire lookout above. Its bell sounded the alarm before falling through the burning tower.
landmarks.timeNote: Fire at the tower around 1:30 a.m.; exact collapse time is not assigned.

landmarks.name: O’Leary barn & cottage
landmarks.text: Catherine O’Leary’s dairy animals were kept in the barn behind the family’s rented-out double cottage. The house survived; the barn burned. The familiar cow-and-lantern story is unproven.
landmarks.timeNote: Origin approximately 8:30–9 p.m.; the cause is unknown.

landmarks.name: Chicago Water Tower
landmarks.location: Pine Street at Chicago Avenue, west side
landmarks.text: The limestone tower enclosed the water system’s standpipe. It survived the fire, even as the pumping works across Pine Street were gutted.
landmarks.timeNote: Survival is documented; no exact exposure time is assigned.

landmarks.name: Chicago Avenue Pumping Station
landmarks.location: Pine Street at Chicago Avenue, east side
landmarks.text: The pumping machinery and roof were lost, interrupting the city’s water supply. The surviving masonry shell should not be mistaken for an undamaged, functioning waterworks.
landmarks.timeNote: About 3–3:30 a.m.; Cregier’s report and the museum describe different damage milestones.

landmarks.name: Crosby’s Opera House
landmarks.location: Washington Street, north side, between State & Dearborn
landmarks.text: A newly renovated opera house was due to reopen on October 9 with Theodore Thomas’s orchestra. The fire destroyed it before the performance could take place.
landmarks.timeNote: Destroyed during the fire; a precise ignition time has not been established.

landmarks.name: Lind Block
landmarks.text: This five-storey commercial building, occupied by a wholesale grocer, survived within the devastated South Division business district. Its relatively isolated riverside position helped.
landmarks.timeNote: Survival is documented; the surrounding district’s timing does not determine this building’s state.

landmarks.name: Chamber of Commerce
landmarks.text: The Board of Trade conducted its commodities exchange in this building, dedicated in 1865. Contemporary accounts describe its roof burning independently of nearby fires.

landmarks.name: Sherman House
landmarks.text: A six-storey hotel faced Court House Square. Accounts describe crowded streets around it and a rescue of an ill guest from the burning building.
landmarks.timeNote: Destroyed overnight; exact ignition time unresolved.

landmarks.name: Tremont House
landmarks.text: This was the third Tremont House, a large brick hotel designed by John M. Van Osdel. Like earlier versions lost in other fires, it was destroyed.

landmarks.name: Palmer House
landmarks.text: Potter Palmer’s grand hotel at State and Monroe was lost in the fire. The museum distinguishes it from an earlier Palmer House at State and Quincy.
landmarks.timeNote: Opening-date claims conflict with popular accounts; omit an age-in-days claim until resolved.

landmarks.name: Field & Leiter store
landmarks.text: The six-storey dry-goods store helped turn State Street into a major retail destination. Some merchandise was removed before the building was lost.

landmarks.name: Chicago Historical Society
landmarks.text: The Society’s building opened in 1868 with aspirations of fireproof construction. The fire consumed the building and almost all of its collections.

landmarks.name: LaSalle Street Tunnel
landmarks.text: Opened on July 4, 1871, the tunnel carried pedestrians and horse-drawn traffic beneath the river. It offered an escape route when the South Division burned.
landmarks.timeNote: A route, not a building. No precisely timed closure or casualty claim is made.

landmarks.name: Mahlon Ogden mansion
landmarks.location: North side of Walton, between Dearborn & Clark
landmarks.text: The mansion survived while neighbouring churches burned. The museum credits both luck and soaked carpets applied to the exterior against flying embers.
landmarks.timeNote: Survival is documented; the placement is approximate on the older street map.
